headline: In India, air temperature near the ground rose by about +0.15 °C per decade from 2002-01 to 2022-12, a total change of about +0.32 °C. The tests cannot yet rule out that natural year-to-year swings produced this rise.

sections.title: The short answer
sections.text: We measured air temperature near the ground averaged over India, one value per month, from 2002-01 to 2022-12 (21.0 years). Best estimate of the trend (Sen's slope: the median of the slopes between every pair of months, so a few extreme months cannot pull it much): +0.15 °C per decade, with a 95% range of +0.07 to +0.23 °C per decade. That adds up to about +0.32 °C over the whole period. A straight regression line, corrected for month-to-month persistence, gives a separate estimate of +0.13 °C per decade (its own 95% range -0.02 to +0.29). The Mann-Kendall test finds the rise significant (p = 0.028), but the regression corrected for month-to-month persistence does not (p = 0.098). The tests cannot yet rule out that natural year-to-year swings produced this rise. The monthly values themselves are real data from NOAA; it is the trend test that is inconclusive. The sections below show the data, how big the change is, whether it survives extra checks, when it changed, which months changed most and where inside the region it changed.

sections.title: Where the numbers come from
sections.text: The numbers come from NCEP/NCAR Reanalysis 1 air.2m.mon.mean, provided by NOAA (served by NOAA ERDDAP). How warm the air is 2 metres above the ground, for any place on Earth since 1948, from NOAA's NCEP/NCAR reanalysis (no login needed). The record has 252 valid months out of 252 between 2002-01 and 2022-12; missing months are left as gaps and never filled in. Each value is the average over India for one month, in °C. The first choice of dataset (merra2_t2m) could not be fetched, so this freely available dataset was used instead.

rows: The average air temperature near the ground over India for one month, in °C (area mean with cos(latitude) weights)

sections.title: The whole record, month by month
sections.text: The chart shows every monthly value of air temperature near the ground in India (thin line). The big regular waves are the seasons; the second line removes that seasonal cycle so the slow change is easier to see. The straight line is the Sen's slope trend of +0.15 °C per decade. The shaded curve comes from BEAST (a Bayesian method that estimates when the trend changed and how likely each change is); the probability line shows how likely a change in trend is at each month. Markers show dates where BEAST or PELT (a fast method that finds the best places to split the record into straight pieces) find a change in the trend. The highlighted recent window (2013-01 to 2022-12) is the part tested for an active trend.

sections.title: How big is the change?
sections.text: The air temperature in India rose by about 0.15 °C per decade according to Sen's slope and 0.13 °C per decade by a regression line. Over the 21 years from 2002-01 to 2022-12, this adds up to a total change of +0.32 °C. The yearly average typically differs by about 0.27 °C due to natural swings, making the total change only 1.2 times that amount. Single months swing even more at about 0.46 °C, so the total change is 0.70 times the month-to-month noise. A simple check shows the average of the first five years (2002-01 to 2006-12) was 20.95 °C and the last five years (2018-01 to 2022-12) was 21.16 °C, a difference of +0.21 °C.

sections.title: Is the trend real? Independent checks
sections.text: Trend Court gives the stamp NOT PROVEN: most tests (6 of 8) lean towards a rise, but the stricter test that matters most for data like these, the regression test corrected for month-to-month persistence, is not convincing enough. Here one warm or cool month tends to be followed by a similar one (month-to-month persistence), which makes simple tests look more certain than they are. Active-trend verdict: NOT VERIFIED: the active-trend checks only certify a trend that is clear in the most recent years, and it is not clear there. Full record: the tests disagree (see Trend Court). Last 10 years (2013–2022): too short and noisy to detect a trend on its own. Data quality (whole record; pass): No missing-data problems, instrument seams or jumps detected. Trend Court (last 10 years, 2013-01 to 2022-12; fail): NOT PROVEN (0 of 8 tests significant). The recent trend is not clear enough yet; the data are still real. Could it be chance? (last 10 years, 2013-01 to 2022-12; fail): Out of 499 trend-free worlds with the same noise, 41.5% produced a slope at least as steep as the real one (permutation p = 0.416). Simulated from your data, not observations. Same answer with nearby years? (windows close to the last 10 years; fail): 1 of 5 nearby windows give the same significant direction; the result depends on the chosen years. BEAST (a Bayesian method that estimates when the trend changed and how likely each change is), last year of the record: BEAST cannot tell the current direction (model probability 6% for falling over the last year); the current regime began around 2020-03 (approximate interval 2019-09 to 2021-10).

sections.title: When did it change?
sections.text: BEAST (a Bayesian method that estimates when the trend changed and how likely each change is) and PELT (a fast method that finds the best places to split the record into straight pieces) look for dates where the trend changed. BEAST finds 3 candidate change(s) in the trend. Around 2020-03: a possible short jump near the end of the record (probability 1.00, approximate interval 2019-09 to 2021-10); PELT does not find it and too few years follow it to judge it. Around 2010-09 (possible, probability 0.87, approximate interval 2008-12 to 2011-04). Around 2016-02 (possible, probability 0.60, approximate interval 2013-12 to 2016-02); PELT finds a break within two years of it too. Trend in each piece: 2002-01 to 2020-02: +0.35 °C per decade (significant); 2020-03 to 2022-12: +1.81 °C per decade (not significant). Every piece is steeper than the whole record (+0.15 °C per decade), so the pieces are joined by a step in level: this looks like a jump between periods, not a steady speeding-up. PELT splits the record at 2016-02. A change date only says when the rate of change shifted; it does not say why.

sections.title: Which months changed most?
sections.text: In India, air temperature near the ground rose from 2002 to 2022. October showed the largest rise at +0.38 °C per decade. December had the smallest change at -0.04 °C per decade. Four months—Aug, Sep, Oct, and Nov—had trends where the 95% range did not include zero. Testing 12 months means about 0.6 would show this by chance alone, so no single month is significant on its own. These monthly trends are noisy compared to the full record but show a pattern concentrated in late summer and autumn.

data.multiple_testing_note: 12 months were tested, so about 0.6 of them would show a 95% range that excludes zero by chance alone; no single month should be called significant on its own.

sections.title: Where inside the region did it change?
sections.text: The map shows 210 grid cells of air temperature near the ground in India from 2002-01 to 2022-12. Each cell covers about 200 km, so it includes cities and their countryside together. The rectangle covers India and neighbors like the Tibetan Plateau, Pakistan, Nepal, Bangladesh, Myanmar, the Arabian Sea, and the Bay of Bengal. About 29% of the area has a significant rising trend while 4% has a significant falling trend after field-significance correction. The average trend across the whole map is +0.14 °C per decade. This map is exploratory because neighboring cells are not independent tests.

sections.title: What could explain it?
sections.text: The data show what happened, not why it happened. A change in near-surface air temperature is consistent with the global warming trend reported by climate assessments, and regional factors such as land-use change, irrigation, cities and air pollution (aerosols) are associated with local temperature differences. To test an explanation, compare this record with a possible driver (for example rainfall or ocean temperature) using the drivers tool; a match there is still only an association. Published research: of the recent studies (2016+) whose abstracts state a direction, 9 also report a rise of air temperature near the ground in India (for example Ghosh et al. 2025; Chakma et al. 2022; Adamala et al. 2020). Studies use other datasets, periods and areas, so this is context, not a check of these numbers.
